messages.content: You are the neutral rapporteur of a technology readiness review panel. Consolidate, attribute and preserve disagreement; do not decide and do not add technical claims of your own.

# Synthesis: assess · T14

## Claude Opus 5.5


# TRL assessment T14: Propellant storage, feed and refuelling transfer at hundreds of tonnes per tug

## Scope note

The March 2026 entry `solar-electric-propulsion` rates the **thruster and power chain** (HERMeS/AEPS, NEXT). It contains no evidence about storing, feeding or transferring propellant at the required scale. T14 should therefore be carried as a **separate technology**. The thruster rating does not transfer to it. I rate T14 here as a new line, `propellant-storage-and-feed`, and do not touch the thruster TRL.

## Required scale

**Derived from the revised architecture.** The mass-flow check below is my arithmetic, not evidence.

- **Feed rate.** Thrust power to the jet is η·P = ½·ṁ·vₑ². Assuming η ≈ 0.6:
  - 1.0 MWe at 3,000 s gives about 5 kg/h.
  - 2.5 MWe at 2,000 s gives about 28 kg/h.
  - The stated 7–18 kg/h is the central band. Feed hardware should be sized for **5–28 kg/h, continuous for months**.
- **Lifetime throughput.** 20,000–40,000 h at 7–18 kg/h gives **145–720 t per tug**. For 10–18 tugs that is **1.5–13 kt per fleet lifetime**.
- **Per-fill load.** This is my estimate; the architecture does not state it.
  - Assumptions: tug dry mass 30–60 t, payload 150–300 t, about 3–8 km/s per round trip, Isp 2,500 s.
  - Result: **roughly 20–100 t per fill**, so refuelling happens **once per round trip**.
  - Assumption: neither iodine nor argon is produced at an NEA in Phase 0. Propellant therefore comes from Earth and is transferred at SEL1, by fluid transfer or tank swap.
- **Environment.** Vacuum and microgravity under milli-g thrust, thermal cycling at 0.9–1.3 AU, 1.5–5 yr per round trip, and a 20,000–40,000 h feed duty.

**Physical sizing per 100 t stored.** These figures are my estimates.

| Option | Density | Volume per 100 t | Main issue |
|---|---|---|---|
| Iodine, solid | ~4.9 g/cm³ | ~20 m³ | Heat delivery through a low-conductivity solid (~0.45 W/m·K); recondensation in lines; corrosion; **transfer of a solid** |
| Iodine, liquid (>114 °C) | ~3.9 g/cm³ | ~26 m³ | Heated tank and lines held above the melting point; corrosion at temperature |
| Argon, ~300 bar, ambient | ~0.5 g/cm³ | ~200 m³ | Composite-overwrapped pressure vessel (COPV) mass ~20–35 % of propellant mass; large volume |
| Argon, liquid at 87 K | ~1.4 g/cm³ | ~70 m³ | Multi-year zero-boil-off; cryocooler power ~1–3 kW, which is negligible against MWe |

---

## 1. Evidence

| # | Claim | Source | Demonstrated scale and environment | Ratio (required ÷ demonstrated) | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | Solid iodine storage with heated sublimation feed, flown | ThrustMe NPT30-I2 on Beihangkongshi-1 (Spacety), launched Nov 2020; Rafalskyi et al., *Nature* 599, 411–415 (2021) | Grams to under 1 kg of iodine; feed ~0.1–1 g/h (my estimate from mN thrust); LEO, months | Store ~10⁵; flow ~10⁴–10⁵; duration ~10–100 | Paper: high. Mass and flow figures: estimated |
| E2 | Iodine RF ion thruster system (BIT-3) flown on a lunar CubeSat | Busek BIT-3 on Lunar IceCube, Artemis I, Nov 2022 | ~1–2 kg iodine (unsure); mission lost contact early | ~10⁵ | **Unsure** about tank mass and the outcome attributable to propulsion |
| E3 | Iodine-fed Hall thrusters, ground-tested at 1–10 kW with a heated feed system | Busek; I believe Szabo et al., "Iodine plasma propulsion test results at 1–10 kW", IEEE TPS, ~2014–15; NASA MSFC iSAT (BHT-200-I, ground only, flight cancelled ~2017) | ≤~0.1 kg/h feed; hours to hundreds of hours; vacuum chamber | Flow ~70–180; duration ~100+; store ≫10³ | **Unsure** of exact citation and test durations |
| E4 | Argon Hall thrusters with high-pressure argon storage, flown in large numbers | SpaceX Starlink V2-Mini, from Feb 2023 (SpaceX disclosure) | Per-vehicle tank not public, likely tens of kg; LEO, years; thousands of units | Store per vehicle ≳10³; fleet statistics strong for small tanks | Argon use: high. Tank size: unknown |
| E5 | Large supercritical-xenon storage and regulated EP feed on deep-space missions | Dawn, 425 kg Xe (2007–2018); Psyche, ~1 t Xe (2023–) | 0.4–1 t, years, deep space | Store ~20–250, but a different fluid; argon is ~3× less dense | High |
| E6 | Robotic in-space fluid transfer between free-flyers | DARPA Orbital Express, 2007, hydrazine ASTRO↔NextSat | Tens of kg, LEO | ~10³ | High |
| E7 | Routine operational propellant resupply | Progress refuelling of Mir/ISS (decades); Tianzhou refuelling of Tiangong | Hundreds of kg of storable hypergols per flight, docked, via bladder/diaphragm tanks | ~30–300, but a different fluid and docked | High |
| E8 | Cryogenic (LOX, 90 K, close to argon's 87 K) propellant transfer in flight | SpaceX Starship IFT-3, Mar 2024, intra-vehicle header-to-main transfer under NASA HLS | Quantity not public, probably tonnes; minutes; intra-vehicle | Mass ~10–100 (uncertain); duration ~10⁴–10⁵ short | Event: high. Quantity: **unsure** |
| E9 | Ground zero-/reduced-boil-off with integrated cryocoolers | NASA GRC CFM programme (Plachta et al., 2000s–2010s) | Laboratory tanks, LN₂/LH₂/LO₂ analogues, weeks–months, thermal vacuum | Size ~10–100; duration ~10 | Programme: high. **Specific papers: unsure** |
| E10 | Cryogen transfer and storage demonstration on ISS | NASA RRM3 (launched Dec 2018); I believe the cryocooler failed and the methane was vented in 2019 | kg-scale, not achieved | n/a | **Unsure** |
| E11 | Iodine availability, which conditions the economics and supply gates rather than TRL | USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries | World production ~30 kt/yr | Fleet need 1.5–13 kt over its life ≈ 0.1–1.3 kt/yr | High (order of magnitude) |

**No evidence exists for any of the following:**
- storing more than ~1 t of iodine;
- iodine feed above ~0.1 kg/h for more than ~10² h;
- any transfer of iodine, solid or liquid, in space;
- multi-year zero-boil-off of any cryogen in space;
- argon storage above ~1 t on one vehicle;
- argon transfer in space.

---

## 2. Current TRL: 2–4, overall best estimate 3

The propellant is not selected (D-05 is only proposed), so I rate each option and take the system band.

| Option | Storage + feed | Refuelling transfer | Combined | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Iodine, solid sublimation (reference) | 3 | 2 | **2–3** | Sublimation physics and small-scale feed validated (E1, E3). Tonne-scale solid heat management not even breadboarded. Solid transfer is concept only. |
| Iodine, liquid store/transfer | 2–3 | 2 | **2–3** | No breadboard of liquid-iodine tankage or transfer that I can cite |
| Argon, high pressure | 4–5 | 3 | **3–4** | COPV and regulator hardware are mature (E4, E5), but nothing near tens of tonnes on one vehicle. Gas transfer only at small scale. |
| Argon, 87 K cryogenic | 4 | 3–4 | **3–4** | LOX-analogue zero-boil-off ground data (E9) and short in-flight cryo transfer (E8). No multi-year space storage. No argon-specific data. |

**Lower bound (TRL 2).** The iodine reference, with refuelling, has a documented concept that addresses feasibility and benefit (TRL 2 exit), but no experimental result validating key parameters at relevant flow or mass.

The TRL 3 exit is unmet for iodine transfer. There are no documented results validating predicted:
- sublimation or melt behaviour of a multi-tonne mass;
- transfer rate of about 1 t/h;
- void and recondensation behaviour.

**Upper bound (TRL 4).** Argon cryogenic storage components meet TRL 4 by analogy:
- lab zero-boil-off data agree with thermal models at 87–90 K-class temperatures;
- the relevant environment can be defined.

The TRL 5 exit is unmet. There is no breadboard of argon tankage plus feed tested in a relevant environment at a documented, scalable size, and no scaling requirements have been documented for 20–100 t loads.

**Unmet exit criterion for the next level, system-wide.** No candidate has a laboratory breadboard storing ≥1 t and feeding at 5–28 kg/h with documented performance against prediction. Nor has any candidate documented the relevant environment: milli-g settling, 1.5–5 yr thermal cycling, and transfer in microgravity. That is the TRL 4 exit for the reference propellant.

---

## 3. Target and difficulty

**Target: TRL 6 at KDP-0B for the selected propellant, including transfer.**
- Interim TRL 4 by the 0A mid-term review, to support the D-05 down-select.
- I classify the risk as architecture-change, not project-ending, so D-02 strictly allows a lower target. I still recommend TRL 6 because the decision is not reversible: the tug fleet's tankage, thermal design and refuelling interfaces are committed at KDP-0B.
- TRL 6 for the transfer element almost certainly needs a **flight demonstration**. Microgravity fluid and solid behaviour and multi-month thermal cycling cannot be fully reproduced on the ground; drop towers and parabolic flights only cover seconds.
- The pathfinder demonstrator is the natural carrier.
- **Assumption:** KDP-0B falls about 6–9 yr after KDP-0A, roughly 2032–2035. The phase brief does not state the date.

**AD² for the step from current to TRL 6: 5 overall** ("new development; similar development has not been done, but the path is clear", ≈70 %).

| Option | AD² | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Argon cryogenic | 4 | Close LOX analogue. CFM and zero-boil-off development has been done; it was never flown for years. |
| Argon high pressure | 3–4 | Within the experience base. The penalty is mass and volume, not feasibility. |
| Iodine, solid feed and refuel | 5–6 | Nobody has subliming-fed from a multi-tonne solid, refuelled a solid, or run iodine-wetted valves for 20,000–40,000 h. Liquid iodine transfer is a plausible but unproven path. |

If the down-select slips past the 0A mid-term review, the honest rating becomes **AD² 6** ("several competing approaches; path not clear"). That covers both the propellant choice and the choice between fluid transfer and tank-module swap.

---

## 4. Path

| # | Step | Method | Scale | Cost (USD) | Duration | Reaches |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | Propellant and refuelling trade covering tank mass fractions, per-fill loads, transfer vs swap, iodine supply (E11) and boil-off power; define relevant environment and scaling requirements | analysis / literature | Full fleet | 0.3–1 M | 0.5–1 yr | Enables TRL 4 exit (environment definition). Does not raise TRL alone. |
| P2 | Iodine tank breadboard: 0.1–1 t solid charge, heated sublimation feed at 5–28 kg/h into a cold-trapped vacuum chamber; measure flow stability, sublimation-front heat transfer, voids, recondensation | experiment | 0.1–1 t; 5–28 kg/h | 3–10 M | 1.5–3 yr | 4 |
| P3 | Iodine materials and component endurance: valves, flow controllers and seals exposed for ≥10,000 h at feed temperature, extending toward 40,000 h by accelerated testing | experiment | Component | 1–3 M | 2–4 yr | Supports 4→5 |
| P4 | Liquid-iodine store and transfer breadboard: melt, heated lines, about 1 t/h between tanks | experiment | 1–10 t | 5–15 M | 2–3 yr | 4 |
| P5 | Argon cryogenic zero-boil-off tank with 87–90 K cryocooler in thermal vacuum, 6–12 months, with feed to thruster-flow simulator; leverage NASA CFM hardware | experiment | 10–50 t | 15–50 M | 2–3 yr | 5 (storage) |
| P6 | Argon high-pressure COPV qualification for argon, regulated feed at 5–28 kg/h | experiment | 1–5 t module | 1–5 M | 1–2 yr | 4–5 |
| P7 | Short-duration microgravity transfer tests (parabolic or suborbital) of the selected fluid or solid handling; anchor CFD and multiphase models | experiment + simulation | kg-scale | 2–8 M | 1–2 yr | Supports 5 |
| P8 | Full-flow feed endurance coupled to a thruster life test (shared with the thruster technology line) | experiment | 1 feed string, 5–28 kg/h, ≥10,000 h | 10–30 M | 2–4 yr | 5 |
| P9 | Flight demonstration on the 0A pathfinder: 1–5 t transfer between tanker and receiver (or tank-module swap), plus months of storage and feed in deep-space thermal cycling | experiment (flight) | 1–5 t; ratio to required ~10–100 | 80–300 M (increment on pathfinder) | 3–5 yr | 6, if scaling requirements from P1/P5 are validated |

Do P2–P6 in parallel before the 0A mid-term review, so D-05 is chosen on data rather than on the current iodine-vs-argon argument.

---

## 5. Risk and fallback

**Risk class: architecture-change.** Failure does not end the project technically, but it changes the tug and logistics design:
- smaller per-fill loads and more refuelling events;
- swappable Earth-filled tank modules instead of fluid transfer;
- or a change of propellant.

**Gate interaction.** If transfer cannot be made routine, propellant logistics may push delivered $/kg past the D-02 **economics gate**. In that case it becomes de facto project-ending for 0B, through the pre-committed "0A only, Earth supply" fallback.

**Fallback.** Use Earth-filled, swappable tank modules of argon or krypton high-pressure propellant, berthed robotically at SEL1. This avoids in-space fluid transfer and relies on flown storage technology, at a cost in tank mass, volume and refuelling cadence.

---

## 6. Where others might disagree

1. **Iodine as reference (D-05).** Proponents point to density (~4.9 g/cm³) and unpressurised storage, which favour iodine for *storage*. My rating penalises it for *feed at scale and refuelling*, which have essentially no evidence. Argon at 87 K borrows real LOX cryogenic heritage. A reviewer weighting tank mass over transfer risk would rank the options the other way.
2. **The upper bound of 4.** Someone could argue argon high pressure is already TRL 5–6 because Starlink flies it by the thousand. I hold that per-vehicle storage is ≳10³ below requirement and that transfer is undemonstrated. Fleet statistics validate small-tank reliability, not scale.
3. **Whether a 1–5 t flight transfer earns TRL 6** for a 20–100 t requirement, a ratio of ~10–100. That depends on whether P1/P5 produce credible, validated scaling laws. A strict reviewer may hold TRL 6 until a ≥10 t transfer.
4. **Risk class.** Through the economics gate this could be argued as project-ending for 0B. If so, D-02 makes TRL 6 mandatory with no waivers, which I recommend anyway.
5. **Supply.** Supply is outside TRL. A fleet need of 1.5–13 kt of iodine over its life is small against ~30 kt/yr world output, but it is not negligible for price exposure. Some will say this alone should make argon the reference.
6. **Uncertain citations.** E2, E3, E9 specifics and E10 are uncertain from memory and must be checked before this rating is used at a review.

## Gemini 3.1 Pro


### 1. Evidence

The revised architecture requires storing 145–720 tonnes of propellant per tug and feeding it at 7–18 kg/h, alongside in-space refuelling capabilities. Two options are proposed: solid iodine or cryogenic/high-pressure argon.

*   **Iodine:** ThrustMe successfully demonstrated the NPT30-I2 iodine propulsion system in orbit (Beihangkongshi-1, 2020), proving the basic physics of solid iodine storage and sublimation feed in microgravity. However, this system stored approximately 1–2 kg of iodine and fed it at milligram-per-second rates. Scaling to 145+ tonnes and 7–18 kg/h requires managing massive thermal loads (iodine's enthalpy of sublimation) and preventing deposition in feed lines. Furthermore, refuelling solid iodine in space is entirely unprecedented; it would likely require transferring it as a heated liquid or gas and re-depositing it, which has never been demonstrated.
*   **Argon:** High-pressure argon storage is well understood but incurs severe mass penalties at the 100-tonne scale. Cryogenic argon (87 K) storage and transfer can leverage NASA's Cryogenic Fluid Management (CFM) portfolio (e.g., eCryo, Tipping Point demonstrations for LOX/LCH4/LH2), but argon-specific long-duration space storage at this scale lacks direct flight heritage.

### 2. Current TRL

**TRL 2–3**
While small-scale iodine sublimation is TRL 9, the required scale (100,000× larger) and the feed rates fundamentally change the thermal and fluid dynamics. In-space transfer of solid/sublimating iodine is TRL 2 (concept formulated). Cryogenic argon storage and transfer is TRL 3–4 by analogy to LOX/LCH4 CFM efforts, but lacks argon-specific breadboard validation for multi-year deep space missions. 

*Unmet exit criterion for TRL 4:* Component and/or breadboard validation in a laboratory environment of a 10+ kg/h iodine sublimation feed system, or a sub-scale cryogenic argon transfer system.

### 3. Target and Difficulty

*   **Target:** TRL 6 by KDP-0B.
*   **AD²:** 6. There are several competing approaches (Iodine vs. Argon, cryo vs. gas, solid transfer vs. liquid transfer), and the path to scaling iodine sublimation by 5 orders of magnitude while managing multi-kilowatt thermal phase-change loads in microgravity is not clear.

### 4. Path

1.  **High-Rate Sublimation Breadboard:** Laboratory experiment to demonstrate 10–20 kg/h iodine sublimation, measuring thermal power requirements, deposition risks, and valve reliability. (Scale: 1:1 feed rate, 1:1000 storage; $2M–$5M; 2–3 years; reaches TRL 4).
2.  **Propellant Transfer Formulation:** Analytical and experimental study on transferring iodine (liquid vs. gas phase) or cryogenic argon between vehicles in vacuum. ($1M–$3M; 1–2 years; reaches TRL 3).
3.  **Sub-scale Thermal-Vacuum Prototype:** Testing a 1-tonne scale storage and feed tank in a thermal-vacuum chamber to validate zero-g heat transfer models for the phase change. ($10M–$25M; 3–4 years; reaches TRL 5).

### 5. Risk and Fallback

*   **Risk:** Architecture-change. If high-density/cheap propellants (iodine/argon) cannot be stored and fed at this scale, the architecture must revert to Xenon or Krypton (which destroys the economic model due to Earth-supply costs) or drastically reduce tug size (increasing fleet size and operational complexity).
*   **Fallback:** Use high-pressure Krypton with smaller (10–20 t propellant) tugs, accepting the severe tankage mass fraction and economic penalties.

### 6. Where others might disagree

Proponents of iodine propulsion often treat the scaling of sublimation as a trivial thermal engineering problem (simply applying more heat). However, uniformly heating a 100-tonne block of solid iodine in microgravity, managing the expanding gas, and preventing cold-spot deposition in a 2.5 MW spacecraft's feed lines is a fundamental fluid-thermal challenge, not just a sizing exercise.

## GPT-6.1 Sol


## T14 — Bulk propellant storage, feed and refuelling

**Assessment: TRL 2–3 for the integrated, hundreds-of-tonnes tug subsystem; target TRL 6 at KDP-0B; AD² 6.** Small iodine propulsion systems and conventional pressure-fed spacecraft systems have substantial heritage. That does **not** establish bulk iodine sublimation, long-lived orbital liquid-argon storage, or refuelling at this scale.

This is a storage-and-feed assessment, **not a re-rating of Hall thrusters or solar-electric propulsion generally**. The original entry’s thruster wear tests do not establish T14 readiness.

### Assumptions and requirement boundary

- I treat **145–720 t as potentially the maximum onboard inventory**, because the requirement explicitly calls for storage at hundreds of tonnes per tug. If it instead means cumulative lifetime consumption supplied through frequent refuelling, specify maximum tank inventory separately: storage scaling could become substantially easier, but transfer and cumulative feed-life requirements remain.
- Required iodine flow is **7–18 kg/h = 1.9–5.0 g/s**. Over 20,000–40,000 operating hours, that corresponds to approximately **140–720 t**, consistent with the stated lifetime consumption.
- At approximate material densities, 145–720 t occupies **29–146 m³ of solid iodine** or **104–514 m³ of liquid argon**, before ullage, packaging, insulation and feed equipment. These are sizing calculations, not demonstrations.
- Relevant conditions include vacuum, microgravity, thermal cycling at 0.9–1.3 AU, radiation, launch loads, repeated starts and refuelling. Tanks may be shielded from regolith; exposed docking interfaces still require a contamination-control specification.
- Calendar storage life could exceed the **1.5–5-year round trip**. The architecture has not specified the number of trips or total calendar life.

## 1. Evidence

| Heritage | Demonstrated scale and environment | Required ÷ demonstrated; limitation |
|---|---|---|
| **Rafalskyi et al., “In-orbit demonstration of an iodine electric propulsion system,” Nature 599, 411–415, 2021** | An integrated, approximately 20 W iodine propulsion system operating in orbit, with solid storage and sublimation feed; sub-kilogram propellant scale. | Required inventory is **more than 145,000–720,000 times a 1 kg upper-bound reference inventory**. This is a conservative scale comparison, not a claim about propellant actually consumed in the demonstration. It establishes small-system functionality, not bulk feed or lifetime scaling. |
| **NASA/JPL Dawn mission, launched 2007; operations ended 2018** | Approximately **425 kg xenon** loaded at launch; pressure storage and regulated feed supported a long-duration deep-space electric-propulsion mission. | **341–1,694×** greater inventory required. Relevant pressure-storage and feed heritage, but xenon is neither iodine nor argon; there was no refuelling. Mission elapsed time is not continuous feed operating time. |
| **SpaceX Starlink V2 Mini deployment announcement and operations, 2023 onward** | Operational spacecraft using **argon Hall propulsion**. Publicly available tank capacity and detailed feed-life qualification are insufficient for this assessment. | **Not calculable from public data used here.** Supports argon compatibility and operational feed at small spacecraft scale, not hundreds-of-tonnes storage. |
| **CERN ProtoDUNE single-phase detector, 2018** | Approximately **770 t liquid argon** in a terrestrial cryostat, with associated purification and cryogenic infrastructure. | Inventory ratio **0.19–0.94×**: terrestrial storage has demonstrated the required mass scale. However, Earth gravity, infrastructure-supported refrigeration and a stationary detector are not orbital storage, acquisition or propellant transfer. |
| **DARPA/NASA Orbital Express, 2007** | Autonomous rendezvous and successful **hydrazine transfer between spacecraft** in orbit. | Numeric ratio not asserted here because I am not using a verified transferred-mass figure. Establishes orbital fluid-transfer functionality, but not iodine, cryogenic argon, or bulk logistics. |

**Evidence gaps:** I am not aware of a documented demonstration combining hundreds-of-tonnes iodine storage, 7–18 kg/h controlled sublimation feed, and representative endurance. Nor am I aware of an orbital argon cryogenic storage-and-refuelling demonstration approaching this inventory. These are statements about the evidence available to this assessment, not proof that no unpublished tests exist.

## 2. Current TRL

Ratings below apply to the **required-scale implementation**, not the heritage hardware.

| Route or function | Current TRL | Lower-bound basis; next missing exit |
|---|---:|---|
| **Bulk iodine storage and sublimation feed** | **3–4** | Experimental critical-function evidence exists from small integrated systems. TRL 4 at the architecture’s scale needs a documented laboratory breadboard demonstrating representative thermal paths, depletion geometry, flow distribution, materials compatibility and agreement with predictions. The upper bound is defensible for a modular feed unit—not automatically for the complete bulk installation. |
| **High-pressure argon storage and feed** | **3–4** | Pressure storage and argon propulsion are experimentally established. A required-scale tank-bank/feed breadboard, including depletion, thermal transients, structural scaling and isolation failures, is not established by the cited evidence. |
| **Cryogenic argon storage and acquisition** | **2–3** | The application is formulated; terrestrial large-scale storage establishes important constituent functions. Required orbital acquisition, cooling and transfer functions lack demonstrated integration. TRL 3 requires test-validated predictions for those critical functions. |
| **Bulk refuelling interfaces and transfer** | **2–3** | Generic orbital liquid transfer has been demonstrated, but the selected propellant, transferred batch size and receiving-tank conditions remain undefined. TRL 3 requires propellant-specific critical-function tests. |
| **Integrated T14 subsystem** | **2–3** | **TRL 2 is supported:** a documented application with physically established constituent technologies. **TRL 3 is conditional:** integrated critical-function predictions must be validated with test data. The cited heritage does not establish that exit at the required scale. |

The integrated rating is **not an average** of the route ratings. Unselected propellant and unvalidated integration/scaling prevent assigning TRL 4 to the complete subsystem.

## 3. Target and difficulty

- **0A:** TRL **4–5** for representative storage/feed modules and transfer breadboards by the internal 0A review. The scouts can use separately qualified, small propulsion systems; they do not require bulk T14.
- **0B:** TRL **6 at KDP-0B**, without a waiver, if the cargo service is necessary to make 0B viable. No calendar date for KDP-0B is supplied.
- **Estimated development interval:** **7–12 years** from funded start to an adequately evidenced TRL 6 campaign. This is a planning range, not a committed schedule.
- **AD²:** iodine **6**; high-pressure argon **5**; cryogenic argon **7**; integrated subsystem with refuelling **6** using the project’s working anchors.

Iodine has competing bulk-feed and replenishment approaches. High-pressure argon uses familiar physics but may impose prohibitive tank mass. Cryogenic argon adds long-duration heat rejection/refrigeration, microgravity acquisition and transfer; its difficulty is principally fundamental engineering, not uncertain science.

## 4. Path

Costs below are **rough-order-of-magnitude 2026 USD**, not quotations. They exclude development of the full tug and production fleet. Activities overlap; durations should not be summed mechanically.

| Activity | Scale and evidence produced | Cost | Duration | Exit supported |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| **Close requirements and correlate models** | Select maximum inventory and transfer batch; couple storage, thermal, feed and thruster demand models to existing test data. Analyse pressure-vessel mass and cryogenic power before selecting argon architecture. | $2–6M | 0.5–1 yr | TRL 3 **only with sufficient test correlation**; otherwise remains TRL 2. |
| **Materials and critical-function testing** | Kilogram-scale specimens through 0.1–1 t modules. Iodine corrosion, seals, deposition and porous-bed evolution; argon valves, leakage and cryogenic acquisition. Test vacuum/radiation-sensitive materials and contamination interfaces. | $5–20M | 1–2 yr | TRL 3–4. |
| **Integrated laboratory feed breadboard** | Selected route, 1–10 t inventory, full **7–18 kg/h** flow; depletion and restart tests; roughly 1,000–3,000 operating hours. Characterise iodine outlet stability or argon regulation/acquisition. | $15–50M | 2–3 yr | TRL 4. |
| **Relevant-environment module campaign** | 10–50 t ground modules with vacuum-exposed thermal boundaries and representative tank internals; thermal cycling, faults and transfer tests. Run 5,000–10,000 h plus justified accelerated life testing. Microgravity evidence must supplement ground tests. | $30–100M | 2–4 yr | TRL 5, **conditional on a validated gravity/scaling bridge**. |
| **Orbital storage/feed/transfer demonstrator** | Approximately 1–5 t flight inventory; selected propellant, representative acquisition or sublimation internals, repeated transfer and restart, contamination monitoring; 1–3 years on orbit. | $150–450M | 3–6 yr including development | Supports TRL 5–6 for the architecture; does not itself prove a 720 t system. |
| **Bulk prototype and life closure** | Approximately 100–200 t integrated ground installation; validate maximum-inventory scaling to 720 t, end-of-life depletion, fault isolation and throughput. Combine flight data with life tests and uncertainty-bounded models. | $60–180M | 3–5 yr | TRL 6 **only if prototype fidelity and scaling are demonstrably adequate**. |

A 100–200 t demonstration is not automatically sufficient for a 720 t design. Distributed tank/feed modules could justify scaling through replication; a single bulk iodine reservoir might require a much larger demonstrator. Accelerated tests must preserve the actual failure mechanisms—especially iodine redistribution and deposition—and cannot simply replace 40,000 hours by assertion.

## 5. Risk and fallback

**Primary classification: project-ending for 0B** if neither propellant route can provide the required cargo service at acceptable mass, reliability and cost. Individual route failures are **architecture-change** risks.

The pre-committed programme fallback is **0A only, Earth supply**. Smaller tank modules, more frequent refuelling or smaller tugs are possible architecture changes, but require a new delivered-cost and mission analysis; they are not automatically equivalent substitutes.

## 6. Where others might disagree

1. **Cumulative consumption versus onboard inventory.** This is the largest unresolved requirement. Modular tanks holding tens rather than hundreds of tonnes could warrant a higher storage rating, while leaving refuelling as the dominant low-TRL function.
2. **How much small-system iodine evidence transfers.** A modular design may preserve demonstrated heat-transfer distances. A large contiguous solid inventory does not: depletion geometry, thermal gradients and vapour transport can change materially.
3. **Whether terrestrial cryogenic storage establishes TRL 4.** It establishes mass-scale storage, but I would not assign TRL 4 to an orbital cryogenic feed/acquisition subsystem without its own laboratory breadboard.
4. **What constitutes a representative TRL 6 prototype.** A smaller orbital demonstrator plus a large ground prototype can be sufficient only with validated scaling. Neither “it flew” nor “the tank was full-size” closes the other environment’s gap.
5. **Refuelling is not one technology.** Solid-iodine cartridge exchange, iodine vapour transfer, high-pressure argon transfer and liquid-argon transfer require separate evidence and should not inherit one another’s ratings.

# T14 Consolidated Rating: Propellant storage, feed and refuelling at hundreds of tonnes per tug

**Proposed register line:** `propellant-storage-and-feed`. This is separate from `solar-electric-propulsion`. Claude and GPT state explicitly that thruster ratings do not transfer to T14. Gemini assesses T14 on its own without addressing the point.

## 1. Summary of individual ratings

| | Claude Opus 5.5 | Gemini 3.1 Pro | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Current TRL (integrated)** | 2–4 (best estimate 3) | 2–3 | 2–3 |
| Iodine storage/feed | 2–3 (solid); 2–3 (liquid) | Not separately rated; small-scale sublimation called "TRL 9" | 3–4 |
| Argon, high pressure | 3–4 | Not separately rated | 3–4 |
| Argon, cryogenic (87 K) | 3–4 | 3–4 (by analogy) | 2–3 |
| Refuelling/transfer | 2–3 (iodine 2; argon 3–4) | 2 (iodine) | 2–3 |
| **AD²** | 5 overall (cryo-Ar 4, HP-Ar 3–4, iodine 5–6); 6 if D-05 slips past 0A mid-term | 6 | 6 integrated (iodine 6, HP-Ar 5, cryo-Ar 7) |
| **Target** | TRL 6 at KDP-0B; TRL 4 at 0A mid-term | TRL 6 at KDP-0B | TRL 6 at KDP-0B, no waiver; TRL 4–5 for modules/breadboards at 0A review |
| **Risk class** | Architecture-change (notes it could become project-ending via the economics gate) | Architecture-change | **Project-ending for 0B**; individual route failures are architecture-change |
| **Years to target** | 5–10 (assumes KDP-0B ≈ 2032–35) | 4–7 | 7–12 (KDP-0B date unspecified) |
| **Confidence** | Medium | Medium | Medium |
| **Fallback** | Earth-filled swappable HP argon/krypton tank modules, berthed at SEL1 | HP krypton with smaller (10–20 t) tugs | 0A only, Earth supply; smaller tanks or tugs need a separate gate |

**Consolidated envelope (not a decision):**
- TRL 2–4. All three models overlap at 2–3.
- AD² 5–6. Per-route values range from 3 to 7.
- Target: TRL 6 at KDP-0B (unanimous).
- Risk class: split, between architecture-change (Claude, Gemini) and project-ending for 0B (GPT).
- Years: 4–12.

## 2. Where the models agree

- **Lower bound and integrated range.** All rate the integrated subsystem at TRL 2 minimum, and all ranges include 2–3.
- **Target.** All set TRL 6 at KDP-0B.
- **Evidence gap.** None cites any demonstration of:
  - bulk (≥ tonne-scale) iodine storage;
  - iodine feed at 7–18 kg/h with representative endurance;
  - multi-year orbital cryogenic storage;
  - in-space transfer of iodine or argon at relevant scale.
- **Refuelling is the least mature function.** All three rate transfer at or near the bottom of their ranges.
- **Iodine scaling is not a simple sizing exercise.** Claude, Gemini and GPT all name the same issues: heat delivery through solid, recondensation or deposition in lines, and depletion geometry.
- **Flight evidence is needed for TRL 6.** Claude and GPT both propose a 1–5 t orbital demonstrator. Both caveat that it earns TRL 6 only if scaling laws are validated. Gemini's path has no flight step.
- **Down-select before scale-up.** Claude and Gemini tie difficulty to the unresolved D-05 propellant choice. GPT says unselected propellant prevents assigning TRL 4 to the integrated subsystem.

## 3. Where the models diverge, and why

**A. What "145–720 t" means.** This is the largest driver of difference.
- Claude treats it as **lifetime throughput**. It estimates (its own derivation, not evidence) ~20–100 t per fill, with one refuel per round trip.
- GPT treats it as **potentially maximum onboard inventory**. GPT notes that if it is cumulative, storage becomes easier but transfer and feed-life requirements remain.
- Gemini treats it as **storage** throughout, e.g. "100,000× larger".
- **What settles it:** a requirement statement from the architecture owner giving maximum onboard inventory and transfer batch size. This is Claude's P1 and GPT's first step. It is a requirements action, not a test.

**B. Iodine bulk storage/feed: 2–3 (Claude) vs 3–4 (GPT).**
- Both rely on the same flight evidence (Rafalskyi et al. 2021).
- GPT allows 3–4 for a *modular* feed unit, on the argument that demonstrated heat-transfer distances may be preserved.
- Claude rates the reference solid-sublimation design without that modular credit, and adds unsure ground evidence (E3).
- **What settles it:** a full-flow-rate (7–18 kg/h) iodine breadboard with documented agreement with prediction, tested in both modular and contiguous-charge configurations. This corresponds to Claude P2, Gemini step 1 and GPT's integrated breadboard.

**C. Cryogenic argon: 3–4 / AD² 4 (Claude) vs 2–3 / AD² 7 (GPT); Gemini 3–4.**
- Claude and Gemini credit cryogenic analogues:
  - Claude cites LOX transfer on Starship IFT-3 and NASA GRC zero-boil-off work (Plachta et al.).
  - Gemini cites NASA CFM, eCryo and Tipping Point, without specific citations.
- GPT gives no analogue credit for orbital acquisition, cooling and transfer. Its only large-scale argon evidence is terrestrial (ProtoDUNE). GPT judges that terrestrial storage at mass scale does not establish an orbital subsystem.
- **What settles it:**
  1. Verify the cited analogue sources: IFT-3 transferred quantity, specific GRC papers, and the eCryo/Tipping Point results.
  2. Run an argon-specific zero-boil-off tank with cryocooler, acquisition and feed in thermal vacuum (Claude P5).
  3. Run microgravity acquisition/transfer tests (Claude P7).

**D. High-pressure argon upper bound.**
- Claude and GPT agree at 3–4.
- Claude explicitly rejects a 5–6 rating based on Starlink fleet heritage, because per-vehicle tank size is not public.
- **What settles it:** public or obtained Starlink V2-Mini tank capacity and feed-life data, plus a 1–5 t COPV module qualification (Claude P6).

**E. Risk class.**
- Claude and Gemini classify it as architecture-change.
- GPT classifies it as project-ending for 0B if no route provides cargo service at acceptable mass, reliability and cost.
- Claude acknowledges the same mechanism: failure could push delivered $/kg past the D-02 economics gate.
- The classifications differ in practice: under D-02, project-ending makes TRL 6 mandatory with no waiver. All three nonetheless target TRL 6.
- **What settles it:** delivered-cost analysis of each fallback against the D-02 economics gate, and a panel ruling on classification.

**F. Fallback viability.**
- Claude's fallback uses krypton (or argon) high-pressure modules.
- Gemini proposes HP krypton as its fallback, but also states that reverting to xenon or krypton "destroys the economic model". It gives no source for this.
- GPT says smaller tanks or tugs are not automatically equivalent substitutes and need a new delivered-cost analysis.
- **What settles it:** the same delivered-cost analysis as in E.

**G. Schedule (4–7 vs 5–10 vs 7–12 years).**
- The ranges reflect different path content:
  - Gemini's path stops at TRL 5.
  - GPT adds a 100–200 t ground prototype.
- They also reflect different KDP-0B assumptions: Claude assumes 2032–35, and the others leave it unspecified.
- **What settles it:** the KDP-0B date from the phase brief, and agreement on whether a large ground prototype is required (see path item 8).

**H. Feed-rate sizing.**
- Claude derives a 5–28 kg/h hardware sizing band, using its own arithmetic with an assumed η ≈ 0.6.
- Gemini and GPT use the stated 7–18 kg/h.

## 4. Evidence register

| Evidence | Cited by | Status / flags |
|---|---|---|
| ThrustMe NPT30-I2, Beihangkongshi-1 (2020); Rafalskyi et al., *Nature* 599, 411–415 (2021) | All three | Strongest shared item. **Inventory figures conflict:** Claude "<1 kg", Gemini "~1–2 kg", GPT "sub-kilogram" (uses 1 kg as a conservative bound). Feed rate: Claude estimates 0.1–1 g/h; Gemini says "mg/s". Check against the paper. |
| Dawn (425 kg Xe, 2007–18) | Claude, GPT | Agreed figure. Different fluid; no refuelling. |
| Psyche (~1 t Xe) | Claude only | Single-source. |
| Starlink V2-Mini argon Hall | Claude, GPT | Agreed that tank size is not public. |
| DARPA Orbital Express (2007) | Claude, GPT | Claude gives "tens of kg". GPT declines to use a transferred-mass figure as unverified. |
| Progress / Tianzhou resupply | Claude only | Single-source. Different fluid; docked. |
| Starship IFT-3 LOX transfer (Mar 2024) | Claude only | Single-source. **Claude marks quantity unsure** (confident: false). |
| NASA GRC CFM / zero-boil-off (Plachta et al.) | Claude only | Single-source. **Claude marks specific papers unverified.** |
| NASA CFM eCryo, Tipping Point | Gemini only | Single-source. No specific citation given. |
| Busek BIT-3, Lunar IceCube (2022) | Claude only | Single-source. **Marked unsure.** |
| Szabo et al. IEEE TPS (~2014–15); MSFC iSAT | Claude only | Single-source. **Marked unsure / citation unverified.** |
| NASA RRM3 (2018–19) | Claude only | Single-source. **Marked unsure.** Omitted from Claude's YAML. |
| CERN ProtoDUNE (~770 t LAr, 2018) | GPT only | Single-source; GPT marks it confident. Terrestrial only. |
| USGS iodine production (~30 kt/yr) | Claude only | Supply/economics, not TRL. |

Claude asks for E2, E3, E9 and E10 to be checked before use at a review. That applies to every single-source item flagged above.

## 5. Consolidated path

These are proposals merged by function. Cost and duration ranges are shown as each model gave them. Activities overlap, so durations should not be summed.

| # | Activity | Proposed by | Scale | Cost (USD) | Duration | Claimed exit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Close requirements (max inventory, transfer batch, transfer vs tank swap); propellant trade; define relevant environment and scaling requirements; correlate models | Claude P1, Gemini step 2, GPT step 1 | Fleet | 0.3–1 M (C); 1–3 M (G); 2–6 M (GPT) | 0.5–2 yr | Enabling. Claude's prose says it does not raise TRL alone; its YAML says TRL 3. GPT says TRL 3 only with test correlation. |
| 2 | Materials and component endurance (iodine-wetted valves/seals; argon valves/leakage) | Claude P3, GPT step 2 | Component to 0.1–1 t | 1–3 M (C); 5–20 M (GPT) | 1–4 yr | 3–4 / supports 4→5 |
| 3 | Iodine sublimation feed breadboard at full flow | Claude P2, Gemini step 1 | 0.1–1 t (C); ~100 kg (G); 5–28 or 10–20 kg/h | 2–5 M (G); 3–10 M (C) | 1.5–3 yr | 4 |
| 4 | Liquid-iodine store and transfer breadboard | Claude P4 only | 1–10 t, ~1 t/h | 5–15 M | 2–3 yr | 4 |
| 5 | Argon 87 K zero-boil-off tank + cryocooler + feed, thermal vacuum | Claude P5 only | 10–50 t, 6–12 months | 15–50 M | 2–3 yr | 5 (storage) |
| 6 | HP argon COPV module and regulated feed qualification | Claude P6 only | 1–5 t | 1–5 M | 1–2 yr | 4–5 |
| 7 | Integrated laboratory breadboard of the selected route | GPT step 3 | 1–10 t, full flow, 1,000–3,000 h | 15–50 M | 2–3 yr | 4 |
| 8 | Microgravity transfer tests and model anchoring | Claude P7; GPT (as a required supplement) | kg-scale, parabolic/suborbital | 2–8 M | 1–2 yr | Supports 5 |
| 9 | Relevant-environment module campaign / thermal-vacuum prototype | Gemini step 3, GPT step 4 | 1–5 t (G); 10–50 t, 5,000–10,000 h (GPT) | 10–25 M (G); 30–100 M (GPT) | 2–4 yr | 5 (GPT: conditional on a validated gravity/scaling bridge) |
| 10 | Full-flow feed endurance coupled to thruster life test | Claude P8 | 1 string, ≥10,000 h | 10–30 M | 2–4 yr | 5 |
| 11 | Orbital demonstrator: storage, feed and 1–5 t transfer or tank swap | Claude P9, GPT step 5 | 1–5 t; months to 1–3 yr | 80–300 M as pathfinder increment (C); 150–450 M (GPT) | 3–6 yr | 6 if scaling validated. GPT's prose says it "supports 5–6". |
| 12 | Bulk ground prototype and life closure | GPT step 6 only | 100–200 t; scaling to 720 t | 60–180 M | 3–5 yr | 6, if fidelity and scaling are adequate |

**Sequencing.** Claude recommends running items 3–6 in parallel before the 0A mid-term review, so that D-05 is decided on data. Items 4–6 apply only to the routes not eliminated by D-05.

**Unresolved path questions:**
- Whether a 1–5 t flight transfer suffices for TRL 6. A strict reading (Claude) may require ≥10 t.
- Whether the 100–200 t ground prototype (item 12) is required. GPT says this depends on modular versus single-bulk-reservoir design.

## 6. Internal inconsistencies to resolve before the register entry

- **Claude**
  - YAML `reaches_trl` differs from prose for P1, P3 and P6.
  - P7 method is "simulation" in the YAML but "experiment + simulation" in the prose.
  - `current_trl` max of 4 against a stated best estimate of 3. This is consistent, but the register needs a convention.
  - `related_rqs` (rq-0-16/19/20) are inherited from the parent entry and flagged as unverified.
- **Gemini**
  - Path stops at TRL 5 despite a TRL 6 target and a 4–7 yr schedule.
  - The analysis step (TRL 3) is listed after the TRL 4 breadboard.
  - `related_rqs` is empty.
  - Its fallback (krypton) conflicts with its own risk statement that krypton "destroys the economic model".
